title: Spring Boot
description: Production-grade Spring: efficient queries, security with JWT, resilience and background work.
resumo: Projections (closed interfaces or DTO queries) for listings; entities when you change data.
Resource Server validates JWT signature, issuer and expiry; authorize with `SCOPE_` authorities. Disable CSRF only for stateless token APIs.
Timeouts first; retry only idempotent calls, with backoff; circuit breaker for persistent failures — fallback on `@Retry`.
`@Async` loses exceptions from `void` methods and tasks on restart — use a queue for work that matters.
`@Scheduled` runs on every instance: use ShedLock.
On Kubernetes, use the platform for discovery and configuration; RestClient + HTTP Interfaces over OpenFeign.

subsections.subtitle: Projections and Efficient Queries
subsections.description: Fetching only what the screen needs.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a list screen loads full entities with every column and relationship, and keeps them all in the persistence context — memory and time for data nobody shows.

**Concept:** projections based on interfaces or records select only the columns used, are not managed by Hibernate, and reduce memory and traffic. Combine them with pagination for large lists.

**How it works:** use entities when you are going to change data; use projections for listings and reports.
examples.interview_question: When should you use projections instead of loading full entities?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: An "open" projection with a SpEL expression. To evaluate it, Spring must load the whole entities, so the projection saves nothing. Use closed projections (plain getters) or a DTO query.

subsections.subtitle: Spring Security with JWT (Resource Server)
subsections.description: Validating tokens issued by an OAuth2 provider.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the API must accept tokens issued by the company's identity provider, reject forged or expired ones, and authorize by scope.

**Concept:** as an OAuth2 Resource Server, Spring Security validates each JWT: signature (with the provider's public keys), issuer, expiry and, if configured, audience. The risks: long-lived tokens that leak, accepting unexpected algorithms, not checking issuer and audience, and putting sensitive data in the payload (only Base64, not encrypted). Mitigations: short-lived access tokens with refresh tokens, validation by the Resource Server, authorization by scope, and a ready-made provider (Keycloak, Auth0, Cognito) instead of issuing tokens by hand.

**How it works:** set the issuer URI and Spring downloads the keys and checks signature, issuer and expiry. Scopes become authorities prefixed with `SCOPE_`.
examples.interview_question: What are the common risks of using JWT, and how do you mitigate them?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Disabling CSRF in an application that authenticates with session cookies. The browser sends the cookie automatically, so another site can make requests on the user's behalf. Turning CSRF off is only safe for stateless APIs authenticated with bearer tokens.

subsections.subtitle: Resilience with Resilience4j
subsections.description: Timeout, retry and circuit breaker around remote calls.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the shipping service gets slow, and every checkout thread waits on it until the whole application stops answering.

**Concept:** retry helps with transient failures (an occasional timeout, a 503): always with backoff, a limit on attempts, and only for idempotent operations. A circuit breaker protects against persistent failure: past an error rate it "opens" and fails fast, saving threads and giving the remote service time to recover, with a fallback when possible. Neither works without a timeout — always set one on the HTTP client.

**How it works:** by default the Retry aspect wraps the CircuitBreaker, so put the fallback on `@Retry`. If it sits on `@CircuitBreaker`, the Retry receives the fallback's value and never tries again.
examples.interview_question: When do you apply a circuit breaker, and when a retry?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Retrying a non-idempotent call, such as charging a card. A timeout does not mean the charge failed — it may have gone through — and the retry charges the customer again. Retry only idempotent operations, or send an idempotency key.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** sending an email makes the user wait two seconds, and a nightly cleanup job should run once — not once per instance.

**Concept:** `@Async` runs a method on another thread and needs `@EnableAsync`; configure your own executor, and remember that exceptions from `void` methods never reach the caller (by default they are only logged — add an `AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler` to handle them). `@Scheduled` runs periodic tasks and needs `@EnableScheduling`. With virtual threads enabled, blocking tasks become cheap.

**How it works:** for work that must not be lost, prefer a durable queue to `@Async`: an in-memory task disappears if the instance restarts.
examples.interview_question: What should you watch out for with @Async and @Scheduled?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A `@Scheduled` job with several instances running. Each instance runs it, so the nightly job runs three times — duplicated emails, duplicated charges. Use a distributed lock such as ShedLock.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** twenty services each need configuration per environment, a way to find each other, and HTTP clients to call each other.

**Concept:** Spring Cloud Config centralizes configuration per environment; Service Discovery (Eureka, or Kubernetes DNS) finds instances dynamically; Spring Cloud Gateway handles routing, authentication and rate limiting. For declarative HTTP clients, OpenFeign is in maintenance mode; for new projects Spring recommends `RestClient` with HTTP Interfaces (`@HttpExchange`).

**How it works:** on Kubernetes, the platform already provides part of this (Services for discovery, ConfigMaps for configuration), so check before adding components.
examples.interview_question: Which problems does Spring Cloud solve in microservices?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Adding Eureka and a Config Server on Kubernetes out of habit. The cluster already does discovery and configuration, so you now run, secure and upgrade two extra systems that duplicate it.
examples.code:
WRONG on Kubernetes: Eureka + Config Server + Kubernetes Services + ConfigMaps
                     (two discovery systems, two configuration systems)

RIGHT: call services by their Kubernetes Service name (http://stock),
       configuration from ConfigMaps and Secrets
